section.title: Changing velocity and the need for limits
section.p: Step velocities were friendly. On each interval, the velocity graph was flat, so a rectangle gave exact displacement and a line segment gave exact position.

Real motion is not usually so polite. A car speeds up while the clock is running. A falling stone moves faster at each instant. A population grows at a rate that changes with its size. The old rectangle and slope pictures still guide us, but now they are no longer exact after only finitely many pieces.
The new idea is to look closer and closer.

To see the pattern, write the nearby time as 2+h. Then
The number h is the time step. It may be positive or negative, but it cannot equal 0 inside this fraction.

subsection.p: As h gets closer to 0, the average velocities get closer to 4. So the instantaneous velocity at t=2 should be 4.
We have just used the idea of a limit. We have not yet defined limits carefully, but the picture is already clear:
subsection.md: \boxed{\text{instantaneous velocity} = \text{the value approached by average velocities over shrinking intervals.}}

subsection.title: The word if matters
subsection.p: The average velocities must approach a single number. That does not always happen.
Recall the forward-then-backward motion from . In one simplified model,
Before t=2, the slope is 40. After t=2, the slope is -30. The graph has a corner at t=2.
If we approach t=2 from the left, the average velocities approach 40. If we approach from the right, they approach -30. There is no single velocity at the switching instant in this idealized model.

remark.title: Condition for a derivative
remark.p: A derivative is born only when the nearby average rates settle toward one value.

subsection.p: This is why calculus needs limits. The phrase gets close to must become precise enough to decide whether one number is really being approached.

subsection.p: Average velocity has a geometric twin: secant slope.

figure.caption: As the second point Q moves toward P, the secant lines approach the tangent line. The slope of that tangent line is the instantaneous velocity.

subsection.p: At this stage, the tangent line is not merely a line that touches the curve. Some tangent lines cross the curve. Some lines can touch a graph without being the right tangent. The tangent line is the line obtained from limiting secant lines.
This changes the question from geometry to arithmetic:
subsection.md: \boxed{\text{Find the tangent slope} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{find a limit of average rates.}}

subsection.title: The area problem
subsection.p: Now reverse the story. Suppose we know velocity and want displacement.
If the velocity is constant on each time interval, rectangles give the exact answer. But suppose the velocity changes continuously, for example
from t=0 to t=2.
The graph is curved. No finite collection of rectangles naturally gives the exact area under it. But rectangles can estimate the area.

subsection.p: Using more rectangles improves the estimates.
Here M_n is the midpoint estimate, which uses the height of the curve at the middle of each subinterval.
The left and right estimates squeeze closer together. The midpoint estimate settles even faster. The number they approach is the area under the curve. Later we will call it
The exact value will turn out to be \frac{8}{3}.
For now, the important point is not the answer. It is the method:
subsection.md: \boxed{\text{area under a changing graph} = \text{the value approached by better and better rectangle sums.}}

subsection.title: Why finite arithmetic is no longer enough
subsection.p: Finite differences and finite sums worked perfectly for step motion.
If velocity is constant on each of finitely many intervals, then displacement is exactly
But if velocity changes at every instant, no finite list of rectangles can fully capture the graph. We need an idea that lets infinitely many improving finite estimates settle toward one number.
That idea is a limit.
